title: Rivers on a table
bodyMd:
Before computers could calculate how water moves, engineers who wanted to know what a new harbour wall or a straightened channel would do to a river built the river in miniature. Whole halls were given over to concrete replicas of estuaries and river reaches, shaped from survey maps, with pumps and gates that could reproduce a flood or a cycle of tides in a fraction of the real time. One laboratory's estuary model, built at a five-hundredth of the true length, was longer than a football pitch.

Shrinking a river, however, is not like shrinking a photograph, because some properties of water do not shrink with the model. A sheet of water a few millimetres deep behaves differently from a river several metres deep: surface tension and the water's own stickiness, negligible in nature, begin to matter, and a flow that would be turbulent in the real river can become smooth and orderly on the table. A model built faithfully to one scale in every direction could therefore give the wrong answer precisely because it was faithful.

Modellers responded with deliberate distortion. They stretched the vertical scale, making depths perhaps ten times greater in proportion than lengths, so that the water stayed deep enough to flow as a river does. They replaced sand with crushed plastic or coal dust, lighter grains that the model's gentler currents could still pick up and carry. Each of these choices made the model less like the river in appearance in order to make it more like the river in behaviour. And each had to be justified: before any new structure was tested, the model was required to reproduce changes that had already been observed in the real river, such as where a sandbank had formed after a past flood.

Most of those halls have since been emptied, as numerical models became cheaper and quicker to run. Yet the discipline they taught survived the move to the computer. A numerical model is also a simplification, its settings are also adjusted until it matches, and it also deserves trust only to the extent that it can first reproduce what the river is known to have done. The concrete has gone; the test remains.
